"Muscle spindle"

They convey length information to the central nervous system via afferent nerve fibers. This information can be processed by the brain as proprioception. Merkel cell Merkel cells, also known as Merkel-Ranvier cells or tactile epithelial cells, are oval-shaped mechanoreceptors essential for light touch sensation and found in the skin of vertebrates. They are abundant in highly sensitive skin like that of the fingertips in humans, and make synaptic contacts with somatosensory afferent nerve fibers. Although uncommon, these cells may become malignant and form a Merkel cell carcinoma—an aggressive and difficult to treat skin cancer. Though it has been reported that Merkel cells are derived from neural crest cells, more recent experiments in mammals have indicated that they are in fact epithelial in origin.

220165: Negative reinforcement is a psychological concept developed by B.F. Skinner, where an undesirable stimulus is removed to increase the likelihood of a desired behavior being repeated. Unlike punishment, which seeks to decrease undesired behavior by introducing negative consequences, negative reinforcement specifically aims to strengthen behavior by eliminating unpleasant experiences. For instance, when a student completes homework to avoid the potential negative consequence of a poor grade, they are engaging in negative reinforcement. It is emphasized that such mechanisms should be used judiciously, primarily for short-term behavioral changes, and that positive reinforcement may be more effective for long-term behavior modification.
